summary: Lays out a vision of how Internet information services might be integrated over the next few years, and what steps would be needed. It is an informational discussion paper.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 1727 is a design paper for joining the separate information systems of the 1990s into one. Its idea is to give every document a permanent name, keep a directory that says where each copy lives now, and let the search systems and the user tools work on top of that.

subtitle: A blueprint for tying Gopher, WAIS, the Web and the rest into one information service.

tldr.problem: By 1994 the Internet held a vast set of files and a budding Gopher network, a budding WAIS network and a budding World Wide Web, all separate from one another and hard to search across.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 1727 proposes four levels: the resources themselves, a service that maps a permanent name to the addresses where a resource currently lives, a distributed system that searches for resources, and the delivery tools that users actually touch.
tldr.outcome: It is an Informational paper that represents only the opinions of its authors and specifies no standard of any kind. Its Security Considerations section says only that security issues are not discussed in it.

facts.label: Authors
facts.value: Chris Weider and Peter Deutsch, Bunyip Information Systems

facts.label: Permanent identifier
facts.value: A URN, mapped to URLs by a directory service

today: RFC 1727 is an Informational RFC that specifies no standard of any kind, and it has not been obsoleted or updated. Section 1 of the memo states that it represents only the opinions of its authors, that it is not an official policy statement of the IIIR Working Group of the IETF, and that it does not represent an official consensus. Its Security Considerations section says only that security issues are not discussed in it.

sections.title: Why an Integrated Information Service
sections.content:
The memo opens with an analogy. The landscape in information tools was much the same as the landscape in communications networks in the early 1980s: there were a number of proprietary networking protocols connecting large but autonomous regions of computers, and it was difficult to coalesce those regions into a unified network. By late 1994 there were a number of large but autonomous regions of networked information: a vast set of FTPable files, a budding WAIS network, a budding GOPHER network and a budding World Wide Web network. Although there were gateways between various protocols, and information service providers were starting to use Gopher as a glue between services, the memo says they were not yet in the golden age when all human information is at your fingertips, and were even further from the platinum age when the computer knows what you are looking for and retrieves it before you touch the keyboard.

The paper then proposes one possible vision of the information services landscape of the near future, and lays out a plan to get there. Section 1 is a disclaimer: the paper represents only the opinions of its authors, it is not an official policy statement of the IIIR Working Group of the IETF, and it does not represent an official consensus.
sections.plainLanguage: The parallel the authors draw is with the early 1980s, when every computer network was its own island. The Internet had become one network, but its information had not: the files, the Gopher menus, the WAIS databases and the Web pages were all separate worlds.

sections.title: Three Axioms of Information Services
sections.content:
The memo lays out the assumptions behind its thinking before exploring them. The first is that there is no unique information protocol that will provide the flexibility, scale, responsiveness, worldview and mix of services that every information consumer wants. A protocol designed to give quick and meaningful access to a collection of stock prices might look functionally very different from one that searches digitized music for a particular phrase and delivers it to your workstation. Rather than design the information protocol to end all information protocols, new search engines, new clients and new delivery paradigms will always have to be integrated into the grand information service.

The second axiom is that distributed systems are a better solution to large-scale information systems than centralised ones. The memo asks whether a million people publishing electronic papers to the net should all have to log on to a single machine to modify the central archives, what bandwidth that machine would need to serve a billion papers a day, and what maintenance problems replicating the archives would raise. It concludes that it seems more profitable to investigate distributed systems.

The third axiom is that users do not want to be bothered with the details of the underlying protocols used to provide a service. Just as most people do not care whether their mail message is split into 20 packets and routed through Tokyo to reach its destination, information service users do not care whether the Gopher server used telnet to get to a WAIS database back-ended by an SQL database. They care very much about how they interact with the client, and they do not want to know what goes on behind.

These axioms force the search for solutions that are distributed, support multiple access paradigms, and allow information about resources to be handed off from one system to another, say from Gopher to the Web.
sections.plainLanguage: Three beliefs shape the whole design. There will never be one protocol that suits everyone. Spreading the work across many machines is more sensible than gathering it in one. And the people using the tools should not have to know or care how the tools reach the data.

sections.title: The Four Levels of the Architecture
sections.content:
The architecture has four levels. At the lowest are the resources themselves, such things as files, telnet sessions and online library catalogues. Each resource can have a resource transponder attached, and should have a Uniform Resource Name associated with it to uniquely identify its contents; where a transponder is attached it helps maintain the information required by the next level up.

At the next level is a directory service that takes a URN and returns Uniform Resource Locators for that resource. The URL is a string containing location information that a client can use to reach the resource. Because a resource is expected to be replicated many times across the net, the client would get a number of URLs for a given resource and could choose between them on some other criterion.

The third level is a resource discovery system: a large, distributed system that accepts search criteria and returns URNs and associated information for every resource matching them, providing a set of URLs that the information service providers, such as Gopher servers, could then select among for incorporation.

The fourth level is made up of the various information delivery tools, responsible for collating pointers to resources, telling the user about the resources those pointers refer to, and retrieving the resources when the user wants them.

The memo then looks at each level in more detail. At the resource layer, a resource is any collection of data a publisher wishes to catalogue, an individual text file, a WAIS database, the starting point for a hypertext web or anything else. Each resource is assigned a URN by the publisher, the URL is derived from the current location of the resource, and the transponder is responsible for updating levels 2 and 3 with the appropriate information as the resource is published and moves around.

The URN to URL mapping level takes a URN and returns a number of URLs for the various instantiations of that resource on the net, and maintains the URN space. Its only required function is therefore the ability to maintain a global namespace and to provide mappings from that namespace to the URLs, so any of the distributed directory service protocols could supply it. X.500 provides exactly the functionality this level needs but does not yet have the functionality for level 3, and the memo notes that the level 2 service need not be provided by a monolithic system: any collection of protocols that jointly satisfies the requirements and interoperates will do, so that level 2 appears to level 3 to be universal in scope.

The resource discovery level is the one that requires the most work and where the memo says the greatest traps lurk. It needs to serve as a giant repository of all information about every publication, except that required for the URN to URL mapping, and since this part is the least filled in at the moment the memo proposes a mechanism which may or may not be the one eventually used. When a new resource is created it is assigned a URN determined by the publisher. The publisher is responsible for assigning the URN from the publisher's namespace and for notifying a publishing agent that a new resource has been created; that agent either forms part of the resource location service or takes on the responsibility of notifying an external resource location service, or it can use the resource location service to find the parts of it that should be told.

The memo gives a worked example: Peter and Chris publish a multimedia document about their trip to the Antarctic with video clips, ask their publishing agent to generate a URN for it, and ask the agent to attach a transponder and to look around for anyone who has asked to be notified whenever they publish something, or who runs a server of trips to Antarctica. Janet has posted such a request, so the agent tells her a new resource has been created, and the agent also finds three servers archiving video clips of Antarctica and notifies all three, giving out the URN and a URL for the local copy.
sections.plainLanguage: The design has four shelves. At the bottom sit the actual documents. Above them is a directory that maps a permanent name to wherever the document lives today. Above that is a search service that finds documents by their contents. At the top are the tools people use, such as Gopher and the Web.

sections.title: How the Delivery Tools Use the Architecture
sections.content:
An information delivery tool has as one of its primary functions the collection and collation of pointers to resources, and a given tool may group those pointers on other information about the resource: a full-text index groups pointers by their contents, and Archie groups them by filename. The memo notes that the URLs being standardised in the IETF are directly based on the way the World Wide Web built pointers to resources, by creating a uniform way to specify access information and location. With just the URLs, however, it is impossible without much more extensive checking to tell whether two resources with different URLs have the same intellectual content, and the URN is designed to solve that problem.

The pointers a given delivery tool keeps to a resource are therefore a URN and one or more cached URLs. When a pointer is first required, for instance when a new resource is linked in a Gopher server, level 2 provides a set of URLs for that URN and the creator of the tool selects which of them will be used. Because the URLs will eventually become stale, as the resource moves or the machine goes down, the URN can be used to get a set of current URLs and an appropriate one selected. Since using the level 2 service is probably more costly than simply resolving a URL, both the URN and the URL are cached to provide speedy access unless something has moved.

The memo then shows what interoperability looks like in practice. Each interaction with an information service either causes a pointer to be resolved, a file retrieved or a telnet session initiated, or causes some set of available pointers to be selected. Once there is a means of mapping between names and pointers, and a standard method of specifying both, the interoperation problem becomes one of handing names and pointers around between systems, although much of the flavour and functionality of the various systems is lost in transition. A system given the pointers can either present them to the user with no additional functionality, or resolve them, examine the resources and run algorithms that tie them together into a structure appropriate for the current service.

The example given is interoperation between the World Wide Web and Gopher, which the memo says happens to be the easiest to resolve. Displaying a Gopher screen as a Web document is trivial with these pointers: a Gopher screen is simply a list of menu items with pointers behind them, which is an extremely simple form of a hypertext document. The other direction is harder: when a user reaches a Web document, all the pointers associated with links off to other documents are brought in with the document; Gopher could then resolve the links and read the first line of each document to provide a Gopher style screen containing everything in the Web document, and when a link is selected the process repeats. The memo is blunt that a lot is lost in this mapping, with some arguing that everything is, but says it does provide a trivial interoperability capacity and that the information content has been preserved across the gateway. Since all resources are identifiable and accessible through levels 2 and 3, it will be easy to copy resources from one protocol to another, since all that is needed is to move the pointers and re-express the relationships between them in the new paradigm.
sections.plainLanguage: A tool keeps the permanent name of a document and the addresses where it can be fetched now. When the addresses go stale the name is used to find fresh ones. That is also what makes it possible to show a Gopher menu inside a Web page, or the other way round, at the cost of losing the features of one of the two.

sections.title: Other Ways of Interoperating
sections.content:
The memo describes a second approach to interoperability: creating one client that speaks the protocols of all the information delivery tools. The UNITE group in Europe has taken this approach, and the memo says it is best exemplified by the recent work that went into Mosaic, a client that can speak almost all of the major information services protocols. The approach has a lot of appeal and has enjoyed quite a bit of success, but there are practical difficulties that may hinder its implementation.

The first difficulty is common to clients in general: they must be constantly updated to reflect changes in the underlying protocols and to accommodate new protocols. If the increase in the number of information services is very gradual, or if the underlying protocols do not change very rapidly, this may not be an insuperable difficulty. Old clients must also have some way of notifying their user that they are no longer current, otherwise they will no longer be able to access parts of the information mesh.

The second problem may prove more difficult. Each of the currently deployed information services provides information in a fundamentally different way, and new services are likely to use completely new paradigms for organising and displaying it. The clients of these services provide vastly different functionality from one another because the underlying protocols allow different techniques. The memo suggests it may very well prove impossible to create a single client that allows access to the full functionality of each of the underlying protocols while presenting a consistent user interface.

Much of the success of Mosaic and other UNITE tools is, the memo says, due to the fact that Gopher, the Web and other tools are still primarily text based. When new tools are deployed that depend more on visual cues than textual cues, it may be substantially more difficult to integrate all these services into a single client. The authors say they will continue to follow this work and may include it in future revisions of the architecture if it bears fruit.
sections.plainLanguage: There is another way to join these systems: build one program that speaks all of them, the way Mosaic did. It works well while everything is text, but it has to be rewritten every time a protocol changes, and it struggles to show different kinds of service in a consistent way.

sections.title: Publishing, Librarians and Users
sections.content:
The memo then considers how people would fit into the architecture. Publishing here means only the limited process of creating a resource on the net, assigning it a URN and spreading the news that it exists. A creator talks to whichever publishing agent they like, whether a personal one or an organisation that provides URN and announcement services to many authors; once a URN exists the creator can give the agent a URL for their local copy and let it do its work, or attach a transponder and let it work out a local URL and set up the announcement. The agent would be expected to ask where the new resource should be announced, which might be a local announcement so that only people in the company can get a pointer to it, or some sort of global announcement, which the memo notes will probably cost a bit of money.

Once the announcement is made, the publishing agent is contacted by parts of the resource location system. Someone running a WAIS server may decide to add the resource to their index: they retrieve it, index it, and add the indexes to their tables along with a URN and URL combination, so that when a user uses that server it can retrieve the resource if necessary. The memo asks where this leaves the traditional publisher. There are a number of other functions the traditional publisher provides besides distribution, such as editorial services, layout and design, copyright negotiations and marketing, and the only part of the traditional role this system changes is distribution, which may make it much cheaper to publish to a much wider audience. Although copying of resources would be possible just as in paper format, it might be easier to detect republication, and if most people use the original URN for the resource there may be a reduced monetary risk to the publisher.

On librarians, the memo reports the questions asked of the authors over a year of discussions. Librarians have excelled at obtaining resources, classifying them so users can find them, weeding out resources that do not serve their communities, and helping users navigate the library itself, and the memo says none of these roles is supplanted by the architecture. The difference is that instead of scanning a publisher's announcements for new resources, they scan the announcements on the net; once they see something interesting they can retrieve it, classify it, set up a navigation system for their classification scheme, show users how to use it and provide pointers or actual copies. The memo says classification and selection in particular are services that will be badly needed on a net with a million new publications a day, and that many will be willing to pay for this highly value added service.

For users, the architecture allows them to see a vast collection of networked resources in ways both familiar and unfamiliar: bookstores, record shops and libraries can all be constructed on top of it with a number of different access methods. One never needs to worry that a book has been checked out, that a CD is out of stock, or that a copy of Xenophon in the original Greek is not available locally, and a user could engage a proxy server to translate resources into forms her machine can use, for example a text version of a Postscript document on a machine with no Postscript viewer, or a translation of a sociology paper written in Chinese. The memo closes by saying that however the system looks in three, five or fifty years, the vision has the flexibility and functionality to start tying everything together without forcing everyone to use the same access methods, and it allows new views to evolve and new resources to be created out of old.

The Security Considerations section is one sentence: security issues are not discussed in this memo.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo ends by asking who does what in this world. Publishers still edit and design and hold the copyright; they just distribute more cheaply, and a permanent name makes it easier to spot a copy. Librarians still classify and weed, but now from announcements on the net. Users get a library that never has anything checked out.

viz.caption: THE FOUR LEVELS OF THE PROPOSED ARCHITECTURE

layers.label: Information delivery tools
layers.detail: Gopher, WAIS, the Web and others: they collate pointers, tell the user about them and fetch what is asked for.

layers.label: Resource discovery system
layers.detail: A large distributed system that accepts search criteria and returns URNs and associated information for every matching resource.

layers.label: Directory service
layers.detail: Takes a URN and returns URLs for the places where that resource currently lives, and maintains the URN space.

layers.label: Resources
layers.detail: Files, telnet sessions, library catalogues, each with a URN and a transponder to keep the levels above informed.

viz.caption: THE THREE AXIOMS THE DESIGN RESTS ON

items.title: No single protocol
items.text: There is no unique information protocol that gives every consumer the flexibility, scale and mix of services they want, so new search engines, clients and delivery paradigms must always be integrated.

items.title: Distributed beats central
items.text: For large-scale information systems, distributing the work across many machines is a better solution than gathering everything on one machine.

items.title: Users want the front end
items.text: People care very much about how they interact with the client, and do not want to know what goes on behind it.

viz.caption: RESOLVING A POINTER WHEN ITS ADDRESSES HAVE GONE STALE

messages.label: URN
messages.note: The tool asks for the current addresses of a resource it knows by its permanent name.

messages.label: URLS
messages.note: A set of URLs for the various instantiations of the resource on the net; the tool selects which one to use.

messages.label: RETRIEVE
messages.note: The selected URL is resolved and the resource fetched.
